questions.q: Meera weighs a sheet of paper on a digital balance and reads 4.85 g. She tears it into small pieces, puts all of them back on the pan and reads 4.86 g. What should she conclude?
questions.a: The mass is practically unchanged: the 0.01 g difference is within the uncertainty of the last digit, and a physical change does not alter mass. The book notes a variation of about one in the last digit is experimental error.
o: The mass is practically unchanged: the 0.01 g difference is within the uncertainty of the last digit, and a physical change does not alter mass
The mass has increased, because tearing creates more surface and so adds matter to the paper
The Law of Conservation of Mass fails for paper, because a physical change can add a little mass
The reading is meaningless, because mass can be compared only in a chemical change

questions.q: In a sealed flask, 8.0 g of substance A reacts completely with 5.5 g of substance B and gives only two products, C and D. The mass of C is found to be 6.3 g. What is the mass of D?

Imran fixes a balloon over a flask of vinegar to hold the gas from baking soda, but the thread is loose and the balloon hisses as it fills. His final reading is lower than the initial one. What is the best explanation?
questions.a: Some carbon dioxide leaked out past the loose thread, so the set-up behaved partly like an open system. Mass is conserved only if nothing leaves the system.
o: Some carbon dioxide leaked out past the loose thread, so the set-up behaved partly like an open system
The leaking balloon destroyed some of the matter, so the law holds only for tightly tied balloons
The baking soda lost its mass to the vinegar, which gained none, so the total fell
A balloon made the reaction stop early, so less product was formed than normal

questions.q: Two flasks, A with sodium sulfate solution and B with barium chloride solution, are left uncovered on a balance. After B is poured into A and a white solid forms, the total reading is unchanged. Priya asks why an open set-up still shows no change. Which answer fits this reaction?
questions.a: No gas is formed: the barium sulfate stays in the flask as a precipitate and the sodium chloride stays in solution. The book carries this reaction out in an open system because no gas is formed.
o: No gas is formed: the barium sulfate stays in the flask as a precipitate and the sodium chloride stays in solution
Open flasks are as good as sealed ones for every reaction, since air can never carry matter away
The white precipitate is a physical change, so its mass is not counted in the reading
The two solutions react only after the weighing, so the final reading is the same as the initial one

questions.q: A group seals reactants in a flask and records 5.00 g before and 4.20 g after the reaction, with no gas let out and no leak. The group writes 'the law of conservation of mass has failed for this reaction'. Which response is best?
questions.a: Reject the claim: a drop this large is far outside the +/-1 in the last digit, so a weighing error or an unweighed product is the likelier cause. The book's own test of the law, in closed set-ups, showed readings that agreed within experimental error.
o: Reject the claim: a drop this large is far outside the +/-1 in the last digit, so a weighing error or an unweighed product is the likelier cause
Accept the claim, because a sealed flask that loses 0.80 g has shown that mass can be destroyed
Accept the claim only for sealed flasks, because open flasks are the ones that show the law
Reject the claim only because the law is stated for physical changes, not chemical changes

questions.q:
Read the statements about mass during changes.
Statement 1: When salt dissolves in water in a beaker, the mass of the solution equals the sum of the masses of the water and the salt.
Statement 2: In a sealed flask in which a gas is formed, the total mass of the products is less than the total mass of the reactants.
Statement 3: When two solutions react to form a precipitate in a closed flask, the total mass before and after the reaction is the same.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only. In a sealed flask nothing escapes, so the gas is weighed with the rest and the totals stay equal.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): When baking soda is added to vinegar in an open flask on a balance, the final reading is lower than the initial reading.
Reason (R): Carbon dioxide formed in the reaction is destroyed, so the mass of the products is less than that of the reactants.
questions.a: A is true but R is false. The reading is lower because the gas escapes into the air and is no longer on the balance; the gas is not destroyed.
o: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true

questions.q:
Match each reaction (column I) with the mass worked out from the Law of Conservation of Mass (column II).
Column I: 1. 12 g of A and 8 g of B react in a sealed flask to give only C. Mass of C?  2. 12 g of A and 8 g of B give solid C and 5 g of gas D in an open flask, and D escapes. Mass left on the balance?  3. 10 g of A and 14 g of B in a sealed flask give 18 g of C and some D. Mass of D?  4. 9.5 g of A and 3.5 g of B in a sealed flask give 8.5 g of D and some C. Mass of C?
Column II: a. 15 g  b. 4.5 g  c. 6 g  d. 20 g
6 g of hydrogen reacts completely with 48 g of oxygen in a closed vessel to form only water. The mass of water formed is ___ g.
True or False: When a gas escapes from an open flask during a reaction, the Law of Conservation of Mass no longer applies to that reaction. Give a reason.
questions.a: False. The law still holds for the reaction; the escaped gas carries away part of the mass, so a balance reading only the open flask shows a lower value.
s: Reason: escaped gas carries mass away; the system, not the law, has changed

questions.q: In a closed set-up like Experimental set-up 2, a flask of vinegar and a balloon of baking soda read 125.40 g before mixing. (a) What should the balance read after the gas has inflated the balloon? (b) If the same reaction had been done in an open flask and 0.88 g of carbon dioxide escaped, what would the balance read?
questions.a: (a) 125.40 g, as nothing leaves the closed system. (b) 125.40 - 0.88 = 124.52 g.
s: Part (b): 124.52 g after subtracting the escaped gas

questions.q: 12 g of carbon combines with 32 g of oxygen to give 44 g of carbon dioxide. A student burns 7.2 g of carbon completely. (a) How much carbon dioxide is formed? (b) How much oxygen is used up?
questions.a: (a) 44 x 7.2 / 12 = 26.4 g of carbon dioxide. (b) By conservation of mass, 26.4 - 7.2 = 19.2 g of oxygen.
s: Part (b): 19.2 g of oxygen from product minus carbon

questions.q: Activity 9.1 (salt in water) and Activity 9.2 (baking soda in vinegar) are done one after the other. Differentiate what each activity shows about mass and say what kind of change each uses.
questions.a: Activity 9.1 uses a physical change (dissolving) and shows that the mass of the solution equals the sum of the masses taken. Activity 9.2 uses a chemical change and shows that the total mass is the same before and after, if the gas formed is not allowed to leave.
s: Activity 9.1: physical change, mass of solution equals sum of masses
Activity 9.2: chemical change, total mass same only if gas is kept in

questions.q: A teacher says, 'Use a balloon in Activity 9.2, but also keep the balloon on the balance next to the flask while you tip the baking soda in.' Give one reason for each of the two instructions.
questions.a: The balloon traps the carbon dioxide, so no gas leaves and the reading can be compared. Keeping flask and balloon on the balance stops the error from small traces of baking soda sticking to the balloon being left out of the final weighing.
s: Balloon traps the gas so nothing leaves
Keeping both on the balance avoids the error from traces left on the balloon

questions.q: Karan says: 'I burned 10 g of ethanol in an open beaker and no residue was left. So 10 g of matter has been destroyed, and the Law of Conservation of Mass is wrong.' Is he right? Explain.
questions.a: No. Matter was not destroyed. The products of burning are gases that escape from the open beaker (along with the air that combined with the ethanol), so nothing is left behind to weigh. If all the reactants and all the products, including the gases, were weighed in a closed system, the totals would be equal.
s: Reason: gaseous products escape from the open beaker
Closed system would give equal totals

questions.q: A student claims that in a sealed flask, 9.6 g of A and 4.0 g of B reacted completely to give 14.2 g of products. Show that this result cannot be correct if the flask really stayed sealed.
questions.a: Total mass of reactants = 9.6 + 4.0 = 13.6 g. The Law of Conservation of Mass needs the products to weigh 13.6 g in a sealed flask. The claimed 14.2 g is 0.6 g more, which is far beyond the uncertainty of the last digit, so the result cannot be right.
s: Products must also total 13.6 g in a sealed flask
14.2 g is 0.6 g too high, so the result is impossible

questions.q: In an open flask, the balance reading falls from 150.30 g to 149.42 g after two substances are mixed. (a) How much mass has the balance stopped showing? (b) Write a situation from Activity 9.2 that fits this result, and say what reading you would expect if the flask were sealed.
questions.a: (a) 150.30 - 149.42 = 0.88 g. (b) Baking soda added to vinegar in an open flask: the carbon dioxide escapes, taking 0.88 g with it. If sealed with a balloon, the reading would stay at 150.30 g.
s: Part (b): a gas-forming reaction such as vinegar and baking soda in an open flask

questions.q: Sodium carbonate reacts with acetic acid in a closed container. Taking 10.6 g of sodium carbonate and 12.0 g of acetic acid, a student measures 4.4 g of carbon dioxide, 1.8 g of water and 16.4 g of sodium acetate. (i) Find the total mass of reactants and of products. (ii) Say whether the law is obeyed. (iii) If the same reaction were done in an open flask and the gas escaped, what would the balance show for the contents left behind? (iv) Does this show mass was lost? Explain.
questions.a: (i) Reactants 10.6 + 12.0 = 22.6 g; products 4.4 + 1.8 + 16.4 = 22.6 g. (ii) The totals are equal, so the law is obeyed. (iii) Contents left behind = 22.6 - 4.4 = 18.2 g. (iv) No: the 4.4 g of carbon dioxide still exists; it left the flask, so the balance no longer shows it.
s: Totals of reactants and products, 22.6 g each
Verdict that the law is obeyed
Contents left in the open flask, 18.2 g
Explains the missing 4.4 g is escaped gas, not lost mass

questions.q: Plan an experiment with a balance, two conical flasks (A and B) and solutions of sodium sulfate and barium chloride to test the Law of Conservation of Mass. Say what you will weigh and when, what you expect to see, whether the flasks must be sealed, and how you will decide whether the readings agree.
questions.a: Put sodium sulfate in A and barium chloride in B, and weigh both together on the balance. Pour B into A, mix, and weigh both flasks again. A white precipitate of barium sulfate forms and sodium chloride is formed. No gas is formed, so the flasks can be left open. If the two readings differ only by about one in the last digit, the difference is experimental error and the law is verified.
s: Observation: white precipitate of barium sulfate
States no gas forms so open flasks are acceptable
Criterion: equal within the last-digit uncertainty

questions.q:
The science club of a school in Hyderabad runs Activity 9.2 twice and records balance readings. Set-up 1 (open flask, so the gas formed can escape into the air): initial 178.46 g, final 177.58 g. Set-up 2 (balloon tied to the flask mouth so that gas is trapped): initial 179.12 g, final 179.12 g. The club has one balance and three more tests for the afternoon: dissolving salt in water, mixing sodium sulfate and barium chloride solutions, and zinc with dilute hydrochloric acid, which gives hydrogen gas.
(a) How much mass did the balance stop showing in set-up 1?
(b) Why does set-up 2 give no change although the same reaction happens?
(c) For which of the three afternoon tests must the club use a closed set-up, and why can it leave the others open?
questions.a: (a) 178.46 - 177.58 = 0.88 g. (b) The balloon traps the carbon dioxide, so no matter leaves the system and the final reading equals the initial reading. (c) Zinc with dilute hydrochloric acid, since hydrogen gas is formed and would escape. Salt in water is a physical change and the sodium sulfate-barium chloride reaction forms no gas, so open flasks are fine.
s: Part (b): balloon traps the gas, nothing leaves
Part (c): closed set-up for the zinc test, with the reason about the gas formed and why the others can stay open

questions.q:
Lakshmi reacts 5.0 g of calcium carbonate with 3.65 g of hydrochloric acid. Group P does it in a closed container and measures 2.20 g of carbon dioxide, 0.90 g of water and 5.55 g of calcium chloride. Group Q does the identical reaction in an open flask, weighs only what is left in the flask afterwards, and announces, 'Our products weigh less than our reactants, so the law fails.'
(a) Find the total mass of reactants and show whether Group P's results obey the law.
(b) What mass should Group Q have found in the flask?
(c) Is Group Q's announcement justified? Say what Group Q should change to test the law fairly.
questions.a: (a) Reactants 5.0 + 3.65 = 8.65 g; Group P's products 2.20 + 0.90 + 5.55 = 8.65 g, so the law is obeyed. (b) 8.65 - 2.20 = 6.45 g, since the carbon dioxide escapes. (c) Not justified: the 2.20 g of gas left the open flask but still exists. Group Q should seal the flask, for example trap the gas in a balloon, and weigh before and after.
s: Part (a): 8.65 g on both sides, law obeyed
Part (c): announcement not justified because escaped gas was not weighed, and a closed set-up is the fix

questions.q: A lab purifies 13.5 g of ocean water and decomposes it completely. Using the fixed mass ratio of hydrogen to oxygen in water, what does it obtain?
questions.a: 1.5 g of hydrogen and 12.0 g of oxygen. Water splits 1:8, so 13.5 g is 9 parts x 1.5 g.
o: 1.5 g of hydrogen and 12.0 g of oxygen
12.0 g of hydrogen and 1.5 g of oxygen
6.75 g of hydrogen and 6.75 g of oxygen
1.0 g of hydrogen and 8.0 g of oxygen, whatever the sample mass

questions.q: Common salt contains sodium and chlorine in the mass ratio 23:35.5. How much chlorine is needed to react completely with 11.5 g of sodium?
questions.a: 17.75 g. 11.5 g is half of 23 g, so the chlorine is half of 35.5 g.

questions.q: A teacher says that pure compound Z contains X and Y in the mass ratio 3:2. Four students analyse samples. P: 12 g X with 8 g Y. Q: 7.5 g X with 5.5 g Y. R: 9 g X with 6 g Y. S: 21 g X with 14 g Y. Whose sample does NOT agree with the Law of Constant Proportions for compound Z?
questions.a: Q, because 7.5 : 5.5 is not equal to 3 : 2. 12:8, 9:6 and 21:14 all simplify to 3:2, but 7.5:5.5 gives about 1.36 : 1.
o: Q, because 7.5 : 5.5 is not equal to 3 : 2
P, because 12 : 8 is not a whole-number ratio
R, because 9 : 6 is smaller than the teacher's 3 : 2
S, because 21 : 14 is larger than the teacher's 3 : 2

questions.q: 2 g of hydrogen is sparked with 40 g of oxygen in a closed vessel. Water forms, in which hydrogen and oxygen are in the mass ratio 1:8. What is left in the vessel after the reaction is complete?
questions.a: 18 g of water and 24 g of oxygen left unreacted. 2 g of hydrogen can take only 16 g of oxygen; the other 24 g cannot combine because water's ratio is fixed.
o: 18 g of water and 24 g of oxygen left unreacted
42 g of water and nothing left over
18 g of water and 24 g of hydrogen left unreacted
36 g of water and 6 g of oxygen left unreacted

questions.q: In a lab, sand and salt are mixed in the mass ratios 1:1, 2:1 and 5:1. Dev says this breaks Proust's law because the ratio keeps changing. Which reply is best?
questions.a: The law is about a compound, whose elements combine in a fixed ratio; sand and salt are only a mixture, so no fixed ratio is expected. The book states the law holds for compounds and not for mixtures.
o: The law is about a compound, whose elements combine in a fixed ratio; sand and salt are only a mixture, so no fixed ratio is expected
The law holds only when the ratio keeps changing from sample to sample
The law is broken, but only for salt, because it is a compound of two elements
The law is broken, because any two substances that are mixed should keep a fixed ratio

questions.q:
Read the statements about Dalton's Atomic Theory.
Statement 1: Atoms can be created, but not destroyed, in a chemical reaction.
Statement 2: Atoms combine in the ratio of simple whole numbers to form compounds.
Statement 3: The relative number and kinds of atoms are constant in a given compound.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only. The theory says atoms can be neither created nor destroyed in a reaction.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Purified water from a river and from the ocean show the same mass ratio of hydrogen to oxygen.
Reason (R): Dalton proposed that the relative number and kinds of atoms are constant in a given compound and that atoms of an element are identical in mass.
questions.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A. Equal numbers of identical hydrogen and oxygen atoms in every water sample give the same mass ratio.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q:
Match each sample (column I) with the mass worked out from its fixed ratio (column II).
Column I: 1. Hydrogen in 36 g of purified water (H:O = 1:8)  2. Sodium in 58.5 g of sodium chloride (Na:Cl = 23:35.5)  3. Oxygen combined with 21 g of carbon in carbon monoxide (C:O = 3:4)  4. Oxygen combined with 50 g of sulfur in a compound with sulfur and oxygen in the ratio 2:3
Column II: a. 4 g  b. 28 g  c. 75 g  d. 23 g
A copper oxide contains copper and oxygen in the mass ratio 4:1. A student has 6 g of oxygen, so the copper needed to combine with it completely is ___ g.

True or False: Dalton's postulates that atoms of an element are identical in mass and that atoms combine in simple whole-number ratios together explain why a compound has a fixed composition by mass. Give a reason.
questions.a: True. If every atom of an element has the same mass and the atoms join in a fixed whole-number ratio, each sample of the compound has the same mass ratio of its elements.
s: Reason: identical atoms joined in a fixed ratio give a fixed mass ratio

questions.q: Magnesium ribbon burns in air to give a white powder of magnesium oxide. (a) Which of Dalton's ideas does this show about the magnesium atoms? (b) If 6 g of magnesium combines with 4 g of oxygen, what mass of magnesium oxide forms, and which law lets you say so?
questions.a: (a) The atoms of magnesium combine with oxygen atoms and are not destroyed or changed into something else. (b) 6 + 4 = 10 g, by the Law of Conservation of Mass.
s: Part (a): magnesium atoms combine with oxygen atoms and are not destroyed
Part (b): 10 g by conservation of mass

questions.q: Sodium chloride contains sodium and chlorine in the mass ratio 23:35.5. (a) How much chlorine is needed for 69 g of sodium? (b) What mass of sodium chloride is formed?
questions.a: (a) 35.5/23 x 69 = 106.5 g of chlorine. (b) 69 + 106.5 = 175.5 g of sodium chloride.
s: Part (b): 175.5 g using the mass of both elements

questions.q: Suppose atoms could combine in any ratio and not in a fixed one. (a) What would a lab find if it analysed purified water from a river and from a borewell? (b) Which law would then fail?
questions.a: (a) The two samples could contain hydrogen and oxygen in different mass ratios, instead of always 1:8. (b) The Law of Constant Proportions (Proust's law) would fail.
s: Part (a): different hydrogen to oxygen ratios in different samples
Part (b): the Law of Constant Proportions would fail

questions.q: 9 g of purified water is decomposed into 1 g of hydrogen and 8 g of oxygen. (a) Which law is shown by the fact that the products together weigh 9 g? (b) Which law is shown by the hydrogen and oxygen being in the ratio 1:8, whatever the source of the water?
questions.a: (a) The Law of Conservation of Mass. (b) The Law of Constant (Definite) Proportions, or Proust's Law.
s: Part (a): Law of Conservation of Mass

questions.q: Students X and Y each make an oxide of the same metal M. X combines the metal and oxygen in the mass ratio 9:2 and Y combines them as 36:8. They claim, 'Our results agree with the Law of Constant Proportions.' Is the claim right? Explain with the ratios.
questions.a: Yes. Dividing 36:8 by 4 gives 9:2, the same ratio as X's. Both samples have the metal and oxygen in the same simplest mass ratio, 9:2, which is what the Law of Constant Proportions requires of one compound.
s: Same simplest ratio, as the law requires

questions.q: A student decomposes a sample of purified water and finds 3 g of hydrogen and 20 g of oxygen. Show that this result cannot be right for pure water.
questions.a: In pure water, hydrogen and oxygen are in the ratio 1:8, so 3 g of hydrogen must be accompanied by 3 x 8 = 24 g of oxygen. The student found only 20 g, so 3:20 is not 1:8. Either the sample was not pure water or the weighing was wrong.
s: Works out 24 g of oxygen needed
Concludes 3:20 is not 1:8, so it cannot be pure water

questions.q: Write a problem on the Law of Constant Proportions for water (hydrogen:oxygen = 1:8) whose answer is 6 g, and show the working that gives the answer.
questions.a: For example: 'How much hydrogen is obtained on decomposing 54 g of purified water?' Working: 54 g is 9 parts x 6 g, so hydrogen = 6 g (and oxygen = 48 g).
s: A question that uses the 1:8 ratio
A correct working leading to 6 g
Checks the other element, 48 g of oxygen

questions.q: A lab has three samples of a compound of elements X and Y. Sample A: 15 g of X with 10 g of Y. Sample B: 9 g of X with 6 g of Y. Sample C: 24 g of X with 18 g of Y. (i) Find the mass ratio X:Y in each. (ii) Which sample does not match the others? (iii) Does this prove the Law of Constant Proportions is wrong? Explain. (iv) Using the ratio of A and B, how much Y combines with 45 g of X?
questions.a: (i) A = 15:10 = 3:2; B = 9:6 = 3:2; C = 24:18 = 4:3. (ii) Sample C. (iii) No: the law applies to one compound at a time, and C is probably a different compound or impure sample. (iv) Y = 45 x 2/3 = 30 g.
s: Sample C is the odd one
Law not wrong, since it applies to one compound and C may be another compound or impure

questions.q: Use Dalton's postulates to explain (i) why every pure sample of water has hydrogen and oxygen in the mass ratio 1:8, and (ii) why the total mass is the same before and after magnesium burns in air in a closed vessel. Then say which single postulate you think matters most for each, with a reason.
questions.a: (i) Atoms of hydrogen are identical in mass, as are atoms of oxygen, and they combine in a fixed whole-number ratio, with the relative number and kinds of atoms constant in water, so the mass ratio is fixed. (ii) Atoms cannot be created or destroyed in a reaction; magnesium atoms only combine with oxygen atoms, so the total mass is unchanged. Most important for (i): the postulate that the relative number and kinds of atoms in a compound are constant; for (ii): that atoms cannot be created or destroyed. Any reasoned choice is accepted.
s: Explains fixed mass ratio from identical atoms combining in a fixed ratio
Explains conservation using atoms not created or destroyed
Names a postulate for each with a reason

questions.q:
A water-testing lab in Chennai purifies samples and decomposes them. River sample: 18 g gives 2.0 g of hydrogen. Borewell sample: 27 g gives 3.0 g of hydrogen. Sea sample: 4.5 g gives 0.5 g of hydrogen. A fourth sample, labelled purified tap water, weighs 36 g and gives 5.0 g of hydrogen when decomposed completely.
(a) How much oxygen does each of the first three samples give?
(b) Show that the first three samples have the same hydrogen to oxygen ratio.
(c) Using that ratio (5.0 g of hydrogen would go with 40 g of oxygen, a 45 g sample), how much hydrogen should 36 g of pure water give? Should the manager label the fourth sample as pure water, or repeat the test? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) River 16 g, borewell 24 g, sea 4.0 g. (b) 2:16, 3:24 and 0.5:4.0 all equal 1:8. (c) 36 g of pure water gives 36/9 = 4 g of hydrogen, but 5.0 g was obtained, so 5.0 g of hydrogen would need 40 g of oxygen, a 45 g sample, but the sample weighed only 36 g. The label should not be given yet; repeat the test, since a sample of pure water cannot show this ratio.
s: Part (a): 16 g, 24 g and 4.0 g of oxygen
Part (c): 4 g expected, so do not certify yet and repeat the test

questions.q:
A salt works near Thoothukudi runs two trial batches in which sodium and chlorine combine to make sodium chloride, which has sodium and chlorine in the mass ratio 23:35.5. Batch 1 uses 69 g of sodium and 106.5 g of chlorine. Batch 2 uses 46 g of sodium and 80 g of chlorine. The supervisor says that Batch 2, because its masses are different, must have made a different salt.
(a) Is Batch 1 in exactly the right proportion? Show how you know.
(b) For Batch 2, how much chlorine is used up, what mass of sodium chloride forms, and what is left?
(c) Is the supervisor right? Suggest how the works should order its chlorine to avoid waste.
questions.a: (a) Chlorine needed for 69 g of sodium is 35.5/23 x 69 = 106.5 g, which is what was used, so the proportion is exact (175.5 g of salt). (b) Chlorine used = 35.5/23 x 46 = 71 g, so 117 g of sodium chloride forms and 80 - 71 = 9 g of chlorine is left. (c) No: it is the same sodium chloride, with the extra 9 g of chlorine left over, because the fixed ratio cannot change. The works should supply chlorine at 35.5 g for every 23 g of sodium.
s: Part (b): 71 g used, 117 g salt, 9 g chlorine left
Part (c): not a different salt, leftover chlorine; order chlorine in the 35.5:23 ratio

questions.q: A lab technician reads the formula N2O3 on a cylinder and writes its name using the prefix rules of the book. Which name should she write?
questions.a: dinitrogen trioxide. Two nitrogen atoms give di- on the first element and three oxygen atoms give tri-; tri- ends in i, so the vowel of oxide is kept.

questions.q: Fluorine has atomic number 9. Two fluorine atoms come together to form an F2 molecule. What holds them together?
questions.a: One shared pair of electrons, a single covalent bond. Fluorine is 2,7 and needs one electron to complete its octet, so each atom shares one electron, as in Cl2.
o: One shared pair of electrons, a single covalent bond
Two shared pairs of electrons, a double covalent bond
Transfer of one electron, an ionic bond
No bond, since a fluorine atom already has a full shell

questions.q: Four substances are written as H2O, HCl, O2 and NaCl. Which of them is NOT formed by atoms sharing electrons?
questions.a: NaCl. Sodium transfers its electron to chlorine, giving Na+ and Cl- held by an ionic bond; the other three are covalent.

questions.q: A student reads that H2O would usually be called hydrogen monoxide and asks why labs and textbooks still write water. Which answer matches the book?
questions.a: A few binary covalent compounds, such as H2O and NH3, are known only by common names. The book names water and ammonia as common-name exceptions.
o: A few binary covalent compounds, such as H2O and NH3, are known only by common names
Water breaks the prefix rule because hydrogen is never given a prefix
Water is an ionic compound, so the prefix system does not apply to it
The prefix system is used only for compounds of three or more elements

questions.q: An atom Z has five electrons in its valence shell and two Z atoms form a Z2 molecule with every atom reaching an octet. How many electron pairs do the two atoms share?
questions.a: Three pairs, because each atom needs three more electrons. 8 - 5 = 3 electrons are needed by each atom, so three pairs are shared (the book asks this for nitrogen).
o: Three pairs, because each atom needs three more electrons
One pair, because each atom is joined to the other once
Two pairs, because oxygen with six valence electrons shares two
Five pairs, because each atom has five valence electrons

questions.q:
Read the statements about covalent bonding.
Statement 1: In an oxygen molecule the two atoms share two pairs of electrons and are joined by a double bond.
Statement 2: Helium atoms share their two electrons in pairs to form He2 molecules.
Statement 3: In water, one oxygen atom shares one electron each with two hydrogen atoms.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only. Helium exists only as atoms because its atoms are already stable.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): CO2 is named carbon dioxide and not monocarbon dioxide.
Reason (R): In the prefix system the prefix mono- is never used in the name of any covalent compound.
questions.a: A is true but R is false. Mono- is usually omitted for the first element but is used for the second, as in carbon monoxide.
o: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true

questions.q:
Match the atoms present in one molecule (column I) with the name of the covalent compound (column II).
Column I: 1. One carbon atom and two sulfur atoms  2. Two nitrogen atoms and four oxygen atoms  3. One sulfur atom and six fluorine atoms  4. One phosphorus atom and three chlorine atoms
Column II: a. sulfur hexafluoride  b. dinitrogen tetroxide  c. phosphorus trichloride  d. carbon disulfide
questions.a: 1-d, 2-b, 3-a, 4-c. The first element keeps its name, the second ends in -ide, and the prefixes give the numbers of atoms.

questions.q: Sulfur has six valence electrons, so one sulfur atom completes its octet in H2S by sharing electrons with ___ hydrogen atoms.
True or False: In a water molecule one oxygen atom bonds with two hydrogen atoms because oxygen needs two electrons while each hydrogen atom needs only one.
questions.a: True. Oxygen has six valence electrons and needs two more; each hydrogen needs one, so two hydrogen atoms each share an electron with one oxygen atom.
s: Reason: oxygen needs two electrons, hydrogen one each, so two hydrogen atoms are needed

questions.q: Neon has atomic number 10. (a) How many electrons are in its valence shell? (b) Why does it neither share nor transfer electrons?
questions.a: (a) Its configuration is 2, 8, so the valence shell has 8 electrons. (b) The shell is already complete, so the atom is stable and does not need to share, gain or lose electrons.

questions.q: A student calls CO 'carbon monooxide' and N2O5 'dinitrogen pentaoxide'. (a) Write the correct names. (b) State the rule that she missed.
questions.a: (a) Carbon monoxide and dinitrogen pentoxide. (b) If a prefix ends with o or a and the element name starts with a vowel, the last vowel of the prefix is dropped.
s: Part (b): drop the final o or a of the prefix before a vowel

questions.q: A chlorine atom needs one electron and an oxygen atom needs two. (a) How many pairs of electrons do two atoms share in Cl2 and in O2? (b) Name the type of bond in each.
questions.a: (a) Cl2 shares one pair and O2 shares two pairs. (b) Cl2 has a single bond (Cl-Cl) and O2 has a double bond (O=O).
s: Part (a): one pair in Cl2, two pairs in O2
Part (b): single bond and double bond

questions.q: Hari says helium should form He2, just as hydrogen forms H2, because both have electrons only in the K-shell. (a) How many electrons does a helium atom have in the K-shell? (b) Why is his idea wrong?
questions.a: (a) Two electrons, which fill the K-shell. (b) A helium atom is already stable, so it has no need to share, and it exists only as single atoms.
s: Part (b): already stable, so it stays as atoms

questions.q: Rina says, 'The prefix rules give the name used for every covalent compound, so water must be called hydrogen monoxide only and ammonia nitrogen trihydride only.' Is the claim right? Explain.
questions.a: No, the claim is not right. By the prefix rules H2O would be hydrogen monoxide and NH3 nitrogen trihydride, and these are correct systematic names. But the book says these two compounds are known by their common names, water and ammonia, so the claim that they must be called by the prefix names only is wrong.
s: Verdict: the claim is not right
Prefix names hydrogen monoxide and nitrogen trihydride are correct systematically
Water and ammonia are the names in use, so the prefix name is not the only name

questions.q: Show that a hydrogen atom cannot form a double bond with another atom to become stable.
questions.a: A hydrogen atom has only one electron, so it can share just one pair (one of its own electrons with one from the partner). The K-shell holds only two electrons. A double bond means two shared pairs, which would put 4 electrons around hydrogen, more than the K-shell can hold. So hydrogen forms only single bonds.
s: Hydrogen has only 1 electron, so it can share only one pair and needs just 1 more for the K-shell
A double bond would put 4 electrons around it, above the capacity of 2

questions.q: A covalent compound is named sulfur hexafluoride. Work back to its formula, and say how many atoms are in one molecule and how many of them are fluorine atoms.
questions.a: Formula SF6. One molecule has 1 + 6 = 7 atoms, of which 6 are fluorine atoms.

questions.q: For each molecule H2, Cl2, O2 and HCl (i) state how many electrons each atom needs to complete its shell, (ii) the number of electron pairs shared, and (iii) the type of bond. Then (iv) say which of the four are molecules of compounds and why.
questions.a: H2: each atom needs 1, one pair shared, single bond. Cl2: each needs 1, one pair, single bond. O2: each needs 2, two pairs, double bond. HCl: H needs 1 and Cl needs 1, one pair, single bond. (iv) Only HCl is a molecule of a compound, as its two atoms are of different elements; H2, Cl2 and O2 are molecules of elements.
s: Electrons needed by each atom in all four

questions.q: Name (i) SO3, (ii) P2O5, (iii) HBr and (iv) CS2 using the rules of the book. (v) A student writes the name of P2O5 as diphosphorus pentaoxide; explain, using the vowel rule, what is wrong, and explain why HBr is not named monohydrogen bromide.
questions.a: (i) Sulfur trioxide. (ii) Diphosphorus pentoxide. (iii) Hydrogen bromide. (iv) Carbon disulfide. (v) Penta- ends in a and oxide starts with a vowel, so the a is dropped: pentoxide. Hydrogen as the first element never takes a prefix, whatever the number of its atoms.
s: Hydrogen takes no prefix as first element
Second element ends in -ide, first keeps its name

questions.q:
A school in Pune prints name cards for covalent compounds on its lab shelves. The cards carry the formulae CS2, N2O4, H2S and PCl3. Software A puts a prefix on every element in the formula, including mono- on the first element and a prefix on hydrogen. Software B follows the naming rules of the book.
(a) Write the names that Software B should print.
(b) How many atoms are there in one molecule of each of the four compounds, and how many altogether?
(c) For how many of the four cards would the name printed by Software A differ from that of Software B? Name those cards.
(d) The school can buy only one package. Which one should it buy? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) Carbon disulfide, dinitrogen tetroxide, hydrogen sulfide, phosphorus trichloride. (b) 3, 6, 3 and 4 atoms, 16 in all. (c) Three: CS2 (monocarbon disulfide), H2S (dihydrogen monosulfide) and PCl3 (monophosphorus trichloride); N2O4 is the same since di- is needed on nitrogen. (d) Software B, since the other gives non-standard names on three of four cards.
s: Part (c): three cards differ; N2O4 does not
Part (d): Software B with the reason

questions.q:
A Class 9 group predicts molecules from valence electrons. Chlorine has seven valence electrons, oxygen six, nitrogen five and hydrogen one (needing one to fill the K-shell). They wish to guess the covalent bonds in Cl2, O2, N2 and in the compound that nitrogen makes with hydrogen.
(a) How many pairs of electrons are shared in each of Cl2, O2 and N2?
(b) What is the formula of the compound of nitrogen with hydrogen, and what is its systematic name?
(c) What name is given to the compound in everyday use?
(d) A group member suggests adding neon (atomic number 10) to the list as an atom that could bond with hydrogen. Is this a sensible suggestion? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) Cl2 one pair, O2 two pairs, N2 three pairs. (b) Nitrogen needs 3 electrons and hydrogen 1, so NH3, nitrogen trihydride. (c) Ammonia. (d) No: neon has 2, 8 and a full octet, so it neither shares nor transfers electrons and would not bond with hydrogen.
s: Part (d): no, neon is already stable

questions.q: A magnesium atom (atomic number 12) transfers two electrons to chlorine atoms. How many protons and electrons does the resulting magnesium ion have?
questions.a: 12 protons and 10 electrons. Losing electrons never changes the protons; 12 - 2 = 10 electrons, giving Mg2+.

questions.q: A sulfur atom (atomic number 16, configuration 2, 8, 6) completes its octet by taking electrons from sodium atoms. Which ion results?
questions.a: S2-, with 16 protons and 18 electrons. It needs 8 - 6 = 2 electrons, so 16 + 2 = 18 electrons against 16 protons gives a charge of 2-.

questions.q: The electronic configurations of four atoms are Li: 2, 1; Mg: 2, 8, 2; Al: 2, 8, 3; O: 2, 6. Which one would generally NOT donate its valence electrons to reach a stable configuration?
questions.a: O, as it has more than four valence electrons. Atoms with fewer than four valence electrons generally donate them; oxygen, with six, gains or shares.
o: O, as it has more than four valence electrons
Li, as it has just one valence electron
Mg, as it has two valence electrons
Al, as it has three valence electrons

questions.q: A student writes that a crystal of salt is made of separate NaCl molecules, each one Na+ joined only to one Cl-. Which correction fits the book?
questions.a: Ions sit in a repeating 3-D pattern, each Na+ surrounded by six Cl- and each Cl- by six Na+. Ionic compounds do not usually remain as single units.
o: Ions sit in a repeating 3-D pattern, each Na+ surrounded by six Cl- and each Cl- by six Na+
Each Na+ shares an electron pair with a single Cl- but the molecules stack in layers
Na+ and Cl- are not charged in the crystal, but they attract through shared electrons
The ions are arranged in pairs and a pair is a molecule with the formula NaCl

questions.q: A store label shows a compound of Fe3+ (ferric) and Cl- ions. Using the naming rule for ionic compounds, what is it called?
questions.a: Ferric chloride. The cation is named first and the simple anion ends in -ide; Fe3+ is the ferric ion in Table 9.1.

questions.q:
Read the statements about ions.
Statement 1: A sulfur atom gains two electrons and acquires a charge of 2+.
Statement 2: The names of polyatomic ions always end in -ide.
Statement 3: Metals generally form cations and non-metals generally form anions.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 3 only. Sulfur becomes S2- and polyatomic ion names generally do not end in -ide, as in sulfate and nitrate.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A chloride ion has fewer electrons than the chlorine atom it came from.
Reason (R): A chlorine atom gains one electron from another atom to complete its octet.
questions.a: A is false but R is true. Cl has 17 electrons and Cl- has 18, so the chloride ion has more electrons than the atom.
o: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false

questions.q:
Match the atom (column I) with the ion it forms on reaching a stable configuration (column II).
Column I: 1. Atom with configuration 2, 8, 1  2. Atom with configuration 2, 8, 7  3. Atom with configuration 2, 8, 6  4. Atom with configuration 2, 8, 2
Column II: a. Cl-  b. S2-  c. Na+  d. Mg2+
questions.a: 1-c, 2-a, 3-b, 4-d. One valence electron is lost, seven needs one more, six needs two more and two valence electrons are lost.

questions.q: A magnesium atom gives two electrons to become Mg2+; each chlorine atom can take only one, so ___ chloride ions combine with one Mg2+ ion in magnesium chloride.
True or False: Sodium chloride exists as separate NaCl molecules, each made of one sodium ion bound to one chloride ion.
questions.a: False. Ionic compounds usually do not remain as single units; ions of NaCl are arranged in a repeating three-dimensional crystal, each Na+ surrounded by six Cl-.
s: Correction: ions form a 3-D crystal, not separate molecules

questions.q: A sodium atom (atomic number 11) loses its single valence electron. (a) How many protons and how many electrons does the resulting ion have? (b) Why does the particle carry a positive charge?
questions.a: (a) 11 protons and 10 electrons. (b) There are more protons than electrons, so the net charge is 1+; the particle is Na+.
s: Part (b): one more proton than electrons, so 1+

questions.q: Oxygen has six valence electrons. (a) How many electrons must it gain to complete its octet? (b) Write the symbol of the ion it forms.
questions.a: (a) Two electrons, since 8 - 6 = 2. (b) O2-.

questions.q: Lithium has configuration 2, 1 and fluorine 2, 7. (a) Which atom becomes the cation and how many electrons does it give? (b) Name the compound that forms.
questions.a: (a) Lithium becomes Li+ by giving one electron to fluorine, which becomes F-. (b) Lithium fluoride.
s: Part (a): lithium gives one electron to become Li+
Part (b): lithium fluoride, cation named first and anion ending in -ide

questions.q: Each Na+ in a sodium chloride crystal is surrounded by six Cl- ions. (a) How many Na+ ions surround each Cl- ion? (b) Why is NaCl still written with one Na to one Cl?
questions.a: (a) Six Na+ ions. (b) The formula gives the simplest whole number ratio of ions, and there are equal numbers of Na+ and Cl- in the crystal, so the ratio is 1:1.
s: Part (b): the formula shows the simplest ratio of ions, 1:1

questions.q: Neha says, 'When a sodium atom becomes a sodium ion it loses a proton, because that is why it ends up positive.' Is the claim right? Explain.
questions.a: No. The atom loses an electron, not a proton. It still has 11 protons but only 10 electrons, so it has more positive than negative charge and becomes Na+.
s: It loses an electron and the protons stay 11
11 protons against 10 electrons gives the charge 1+

questions.q: Show that a compound with the formula NaCl2 cannot be electrically neutral if it is made from Na+ and Cl- ions.
questions.a: Na+ carries 1+ and each Cl- carries 1-. In NaCl2 the total charge would be (+1) + 2 x (-1) = -1, which is not zero. The positive and negative charges must balance, so one Na+ goes with one Cl- only.
s: Concludes the charges must balance, so NaCl

questions.q: A cation has 12 protons and 10 electrons. An anion has 17 protons and 18 electrons. Work out the charge on each, name them from Table 9.1 and give the number of each ion in the compound they make.
questions.a: The cation has charge 2+ (magnesium, Mg2+) and the anion 1- (chloride, Cl-). Two Cl- are needed for each Mg2+, so the compound is magnesium chloride, MgCl2.
s: Two chloride ions per magnesium ion

questions.q: Describe how (i) magnesium chloride and (ii) sodium sulfide form from their atoms: say which atom loses and which gains electrons, how many, which ions result, and how many of each ion combine. Then (iii) say what holds the ions together.
questions.a: (i) Mg loses two electrons to form Mg2+; each Cl gains one to form Cl-, so one Mg2+ combines with two Cl-. (ii) Each Na loses one electron to form Na+; S gains two to form S2-, so two Na+ combine with one S2-. (iii) The electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions, an ionic bond.
s: Mg loses 2, Cl gains 1, ions formed
Na loses 1, S gains 2, ions formed

questions.q: Say whether each of (i) CaO, (ii) CS2, (iii) K2S and (iv) PCl3 is ionic or covalent, giving the type of elements that combine. (v) Write the name of each ionic compound.
questions.a: (i) Ionic: metal calcium with non-metal oxygen. (ii) Covalent: two non-metals. (iii) Ionic: metal potassium with non-metal sulfur. (iv) Covalent: two non-metals. (v) Calcium oxide and potassium sulfide.
s: CaO ionic with metal and non-metal
Names calcium oxide and potassium sulfide

questions.q:
A school science club builds a model of a tiny sodium chloride crystal from 60 spheres, taking each sphere as one ion, and keeping the crystal electrically neutral. Later it plans a magnesium chloride model.
(a) How many Na+ and how many Cl- ions are in the model?
(b) How many electrons were transferred from sodium to chlorine to form it?
(c) For the magnesium chloride model the club has 100 spheres to use and a neutral model needs Mg2+ and Cl- in the ratio 1:2. What is the largest neutral model it can build and how many spheres are left?
(d) A member wants to use all 100 spheres anyway by adding one extra Cl-. Should the club agree? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) 30 Na+ and 30 Cl-. (b) 30 electrons. (c) 33 Mg2+ and 66 Cl-, 99 spheres, with 1 left. (d) No: one extra Cl- leaves the model with a charge of 1-, so it is no longer neutral.
s: Part (d): no, the extra Cl- gives a net charge of 1-

questions.q:
A chemist at a testing centre in Hyderabad identifies the ions in a white solid. One ion has 20 protons and 18 electrons. The other has 17 protons and 18 electrons. The report lists them as 'two ions with the same number of electrons'.
(a) What is the charge on each ion?
(b) Using Table 9.1, name the ions and give the number of each in the simplest ratio.
(c) Give the name of the compound.
(d) A trainee says the two ions with equal electron counts would not attract. Decide whether the electron count matters for the bond and say what does hold the ions.
questions.a: (a) 20 - 18 = 2+ on the first and 17 - 18 = 1- on the second. (b) Calcium ion Ca2+ and chloride ion Cl-, in the ratio 1:2. (c) Calcium chloride. (d) No: the bond depends on opposite charges, not on equal electron counts; the electrostatic force of attraction between Ca2+ and Cl- is the ionic bond.
s: Part (b): Ca2+ and Cl- in the ratio 1:2
Part (d): opposite charges give the electrostatic attraction, not electron count

questions.q: A store-room register records a compound of Fe3+ and SO4 2- ions. Which formula results from the criss-cross method?
questions.a: Fe2(SO4)3. Criss-crossing 3 and 2 gives Fe2 and (SO4)3, with brackets as three sulfate ions are present.

questions.q: A student combines K+ with CO3 2- by the criss-cross method. What is the formula of the compound?
questions.a: K2CO3. The 2 goes to potassium; carbonate gets subscript 1, so it is not written and no bracket is needed.

questions.q: Four students write formulae for ionic compounds. Which formula is NOT correctly written?
questions.a: AlOH3. Three hydroxide ions need a bracket: Al(OH)3, not AlOH3 which would show only one O and 3 H.

questions.q: Criss-crossing Mg2+ and O2- gives Mg2O2 on a student's page. What should she do with it?
questions.a: Divide both subscripts by 2 and write MgO, as the formula shows the simplest ratio. After criss-crossing, subscripts are divided by a common factor if any.
o: Divide both subscripts by 2 and write MgO, as the formula shows the simplest ratio
Keep Mg2O2, since the criss-cross answer is always final
Write MgO2, since the oxide ion has the larger charge
Write Mg2O, as the metal must carry the larger subscript

questions.q: An element A has valency 3 and oxygen has valency 2. Using the criss-cross method, what is the formula of their compound?
questions.a: A2O3. The valency 3 of A becomes the subscript of oxygen and the valency 2 of oxygen becomes the subscript of A, with no common factor to remove.

questions.q:
Read the statements about writing ionic formulae.
Statement 1: The charges on the ions are written in the formula of the compound.
Statement 2: Mg2O2, obtained by criss-crossing, is written simply as MgO.
Statement 3: Brackets are needed even when only one polyatomic anion is present.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 only. Charges are not shown in a formula, and brackets are not required for a single polyatomic ion.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The formula of aluminium sulfate is written Al2(SO4)3, with a bracket round SO4.
Reason (R): Sulfate is a polyatomic ion, and a bracket is needed whenever more than one unit of such an ion is present.
questions.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A. Three sulfate ions are needed, and because sulfate is a group of atoms the bracket shows that the subscript 3 applies to the whole group.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q:
Match each pair of ions (column I) with the total number of atoms in one formula unit of the compound (column II).
Column I: 1. Ca2+ and Cl-  2. Al3+ and O2-  3. Ag+ and SO4 2-  4. Al3+ and SO4 2-
Column II: a. 3  b. 5  c. 7  d. 17
questions.a: 1-a, 2-b, 3-c, 4-d. CaCl2 has 3, Al2O3 has 5, Ag2SO4 has 2+1+4 = 7 and Al2(SO4)3 has 2+3x5 = 17 atoms.

questions.q: Counting the atoms inside the bracket and the subscript in Al2(SO4)3, one formula unit of aluminium sulfate contains ___ oxygen atoms.
True or False: The formula of potassium carbonate is K2CO3, written without a bracket, because only one carbonate ion is present.
questions.a: True. K+ and CO3 2- criss-cross to K2(CO3)1; a subscript 1 is not written and brackets are used only when two or more polyatomic ions of the same type are present.
s: Reason: one carbonate ion, so no bracket and no subscript

questions.q: Write the formula of calcium nitrate from the ions Ca2+ and NO3-. (a) Give the formula. (b) Why does the nitrate part carry a bracket?
questions.a: (a) Ca(NO3)2. (b) Two nitrate ions are present, and a bracket is used when two or more polyatomic ions of the same type occur.
s: Part (b): two nitrate ions need a bracket

questions.q: Write by the criss-cross method the formula of (a) zinc sulfate, from Zn2+ and SO4 2-, and (b) ammonium sulfate, from NH4+ and SO4 2-.
questions.a: (a) Zn2(SO4)2 simplifies to ZnSO4. (b) (NH4)2SO4, with a bracket round NH4.

questions.q: Use valencies H = 1, S = 2 and C = 4. (a) Write the formulae of the covalent compounds of hydrogen with sulfur and of carbon with hydrogen. (b) Why is the subscript 1 not written?
questions.a: (a) H2S and CH4. (b) When the valency after criss-crossing is one, the subscript is not written.

questions.q: Ravi writes calcium hydroxide as CaOH2. (a) Write the correct formula. (b) What does his version wrongly show?
questions.a: (a) Ca(OH)2. (b) Without a bracket the 2 applies only to hydrogen, so it shows one hydroxide O joined with two H instead of two whole OH- ions.
s: Part (b): the 2 applies only to H without the bracket

questions.q: Rahul says, 'Al2O3 can be simplified further to AlO, since a chemical formula shows the simplest ratio.' Is he right? Explain.
questions.a: No. The subscripts 2 and 3 have no common factor other than 1, so Al2O3 cannot be divided further. Writing AlO would give charges 3+ and 2-, which do not balance.
s: AlO would not balance the charges 3+ and 2-

questions.q: Show that Ca(OH)3 cannot be the formula of calcium hydroxide.
questions.a: Ca2+ carries +2 and OH- carries -1. In Ca(OH)3 the total charge would be +2 + 3 x (-1) = -1, not zero. The compound must be neutral, so two hydroxide ions are needed: Ca(OH)2.

questions.q: A compound of aluminium (Al3+) and an anion X has the formula Al2X3. Find the charge on X and name two anions from Table 9.1 that fit it, writing the formulae they give.
questions.a: The 3 of the subscript is the charge of X, so X is 2-. Examples: O2- gives Al2O3; S2- gives Al2S3; SO4 2- gives Al2(SO4)3; CO3 2- gives Al2(CO3)3.
s: Two valid anions named from the table
Correct formulae including brackets for polyatomic ions

questions.q: Write by the criss-cross method the formulae of (i) Zn2+ and Cl-, (ii) Cu+ and O2-, (iii) Fe3+ and SO4 2-, (iv) Ba2+ and OH-, (v) Ba2+ and SO4 2-. Then say which formulae need brackets and which needed simplification.
questions.a: (i) ZnCl2. (ii) Cu2O. (iii) Fe2(SO4)3. (iv) Ba(OH)2. (v) Ba2(SO4)2 simplifies to BaSO4. Brackets are needed in (iii) and (iv). Simplification was needed in (v).

questions.q: A formula app prints (i) NaSO4 for sodium sulfate, (ii) Mg2O2 for magnesium oxide, (iii) AlOH3 for aluminium hydroxide, and (iv) CaCO3 for calcium carbonate. Judge each as correct or wrong, correct the wrong ones, and (v) state the one test that catches every error.
questions.a: (i) Wrong: Na+ and SO4 2- give Na2SO4. (ii) Wrong: simplify to MgO. (iii) Wrong: Al(OH)3. (iv) Correct (Ca2(CO3)2 simplified). (v) The total positive charge must equal the total negative charge in the formula.
s: (iii) corrected to Al(OH)3 and (iv) judged correct

questions.q:
A school lab in Nagpur stocks three metal ions: Na+, Mg2+ and Al3+. They are available as sulfates and as chlorides. A chloride-ion experiment needs 1200 chloride ions. Invented prices per 100 formula units are NaCl at Rs 2, MgCl2 at Rs 5 and AlCl3 at Rs 7.
(a) Write the formulae of the three sulfates.
(b) Find the number of atoms in one formula unit of each sulfate.
(c) How many formula units of each chloride supply 1200 chloride ions, and what does each cost?
(d) Which chloride should be bought if only the cost matters, and what other point would change your choice?
questions.a: (a) Na2SO4, MgSO4, Al2(SO4)3. (b) 7, 6 and 17 atoms. (c) NaCl 1200 units costs Rs 24; MgCl2 600 units costs Rs 30; AlCl3 400 units costs Rs 28. (d) NaCl is cheapest, but if the experiment needs a particular cation (such as Mg2+ or Al3+) that need would override cost.
s: Part (d): NaCl on cost; cation requirement may override

questions.q:
A student's homework on ionic formulae reads: (1) CaCl, (2) Al3O2, (3) Mg(OH)2, (4) NaSO4. Her teacher wants her to find the pattern behind the errors, not only the corrections.
(a) Which of the four formulae is correct?
(b) Write the corrected formulae for the wrong ones.
(c) What is the net charge on a formula unit of Al3O2 as written, using Al3+ and O2-?
(d) Suggest one check that she can apply to every formula before submitting, and say whether it would have caught all three errors.
questions.a: (a) Mg(OH)2 only. (b) CaCl2, Al2O3 and Na2SO4. (c) 3 x (+3) + 2 x (-2) = +5. (d) Check that total positive charge equals total negative charge; it catches all three, as CaCl is +1, Al3O2 is +5 and NaSO4 is -1.
s: Part (d): charge balance test, which exposes all three

questions.q: A student tests a white crystalline solid. The bulb stays off with the dry solid, the solid dissolves in water, the bulb glows with the solution, and the solid does not dissolve in kerosene. What is the best conclusion?
questions.a: It is an ionic compound. It conducts only when dissolved because its ions are then free to move, and it dissolves in water but not in kerosene.
o: Covalent compound, since it dissolved in water
Covalent compound, since the dry solid did not conduct

questions.q: Sample X dissolves in kerosene and petrol but not in water, melts at a low temperature and does not light the bulb in any form. Camphor and naphthalene behave like this. Which statement explains the bulb?
questions.a: X is covalent and gives no ions, so nothing carries charge.
o: X is covalent and gives no ions
X is ionic but its ions are held in fixed positions by strong forces
X is ionic and the bulb or battery used must have been faulty
X dissolves only in flammable liquids, and these block the current

questions.q: A fertiliser shop lists magnesium nitrate, Mg(NO3)2. Using Mg = 24 u, N = 14 u and O = 16 u, what is its formula unit mass?
questions.a: 148 u. The bracket multiplies N and O by 2: 24 + 2 x (14 + 48) = 148 u. Ignoring the bracket gives 86 u.

questions.q: Sugar dissolves well in water, yet a bulb connected to the sugar solution does not glow. Which reading of this result is correct?
questions.a: Sugar is covalent; its molecules dissolve whole and give no ions, so water-solubility alone does not show a compound is ionic.
o: Sugar is covalent and gives no ions
Sugar is ionic but its ions cancel each other out once in water
Sugar did not really dissolve in the water at all, so nothing was tested
Sugar solution conducts, but too weakly to light a bulb on a 9 V battery

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: Molten sodium chloride is expected to conduct electricity, because its ions are then free to move.
Statement 2: A compound that dissolves in water must be ionic.
Statement 3: The molecular mass of methane, CH4, is 16 u (C = 12 u, H = 1 u).
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only. Statement 2 is false: sugar dissolves in water but is covalent and gives no ions.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Ionic compounds generally have high melting and boiling points.
Reason (R): Ionic compounds conduct electricity when dissolved in water.
questions.a: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A. High melting points arise from strong inter-ionic attractions; conduction in solution is a separate property.
o: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q:
A student computes masses with H = 1 u, C = 12 u, O = 16 u, Na = 23 u, Mg = 24 u, K = 39 u, Cl = 35.5 u. Match each compound (column I) with its mass (column II).
Column I: 1. CH4  2. KCl  3. Mg(OH)2  4. Na2O
Column II: a. 16 u  b. 74.5 u  c. 58 u  d. 62 u
With Ca = 40 u and Cl = 35.5 u, the formula unit mass of calcium chloride, CaCl2, is ___ u.

A student tests camphor and sodium chloride with the Activity 9.4 set-up. (a) Which of the two dissolves in kerosene, and which lights the bulb when dissolved in water? (b) Name the kind of bond each has.
questions.a: (a) Camphor dissolves in kerosene; sodium chloride lights the bulb in water solution. (b) Camphor has covalent bonds (shared electrons); sodium chloride has ionic bonds (transfer of electrons).
s: Part (a): camphor in kerosene, sodium chloride lights bulb in solution
Part (b): covalent for camphor, ionic for sodium chloride

questions.q: Using H = 1 u, C = 12 u, N = 14 u and O = 16 u: (a) find the molecular mass of nitric acid, HNO3; (b) find how many times heavier an HNO3 molecule is than a CH4 molecule, to two decimal places.
s: Part (a): 63 u from summing every atom

questions.q: Sodium chloride has a mass of 58.5 in atomic mass units (Na = 23 u, Cl = 35.5 u). (a) Show the working. (b) Why is this called a formula unit mass, not a molecular mass?
questions.a: (a) 23 + 35.5 = 58.5 u. (b) Ionic compounds form 3-D crystals of ions and do not form molecules, so the mass of the simplest ion ratio (one formula unit) is used.
s: Part (b): ionic compounds make 3-D crystals, not molecules

questions.q: A solid is tested twice: the dry solid fails to light the bulb, but its water solution lights it. Predict, with a reason, whether the same compound heated until molten would light the bulb (a) and say what this tells you about the ions in the dry solid (b).
questions.a: (a) The molten compound would light the bulb, since melting frees the ions to move. (b) In the dry solid the ions are held in fixed positions by strong forces.
s: Part (a): molten conducts because ions are free to move
Part (b): ions fixed in the solid by strong forces

questions.q: True or False: A bulb stays off with dry sodium chloride crystals, yet molten sodium chloride is expected to light it, because melting frees the ions to move.
questions.a: True. In the crystal the ions sit in fixed positions; once molten they can move and carry charge.
s: Reason: ions fixed in solid, free to move when molten

questions.q: Meena says, 'Sugar dissolves in water, so sugar must be an ionic compound.' Is she right? Use the Activity 9.4 evidence.
questions.a: No. Sugar dissolves in water but its solution does not conduct, because it gives no ions in solution. It is a covalent compound; solubility in water alone does not prove ionic bonding.
s: Sugar solution does not light the bulb, no ions
Sugar is covalent; water-solubility alone does not prove ionic

questions.q: A student reports a solid that does not dissolve in water, dissolves in kerosene, and whose 'water solution' lights the bulb. Show that these three reports cannot all be true for one compound.
questions.a: Dissolving in kerosene but not in water is the behaviour of covalent compounds, which give no ions and do not conduct. The solid also does not dissolve in water, so it has no water solution to conduct. A conducting solution needs free ions, so the reports contradict one another.
s: Kerosene-soluble and water-insoluble points to covalent
Covalent compounds give no ions, so no conduction
Contradiction stated: no water solution and no ions

questions.q: Using Ca = 40 u, N = 14 u, O = 16 u and C = 12 u: find the total mass of 5 formula units of Ca(NO3)2 and of 12 molecules of CO2, and say by how much the first exceeds the second.
questions.a: Ca(NO3)2 = 40 + 2 x 62 = 164 u, so 5 units = 820 u. CO2 = 44 u, so 12 molecules = 528 u. Difference = 292 u.

questions.q: Four samples are tested as in Activity 9.4. P: dissolves in water, not in kerosene; bulb off when dry, on in solution. Q: dissolves in kerosene and petrol, not in water; bulb off in every test. R: dissolves in water; bulb off dry and off in solution. S: dissolves in water, not petrol; bulb off dry, on in solution; mass of one formula unit read as 58.5 u (Na = 23 u, Cl = 35.5 u). (a) Classify P, Q and R as ionic or covalent. (b) Explain why R is not ionic although it dissolves in water. (c) Identify S and show the calculation. (d) Explain why dry P and S do not light the bulb.
questions.a: (a) P ionic; Q covalent; R covalent. (b) R dissolves as whole molecules and gives no ions, as sugar does. (c) S is NaCl: 23 + 35.5 = 58.5 u. (d) In the dry solid the ions are held in fixed positions by strong forces, so no charge can move.
s: Part (a): P ionic, Q and R covalent
Part (b): R gives no ions in solution
Part (d): ions fixed in the solid by strong forces

questions.q: A student's notebook says: (i) formula unit mass of Na2O = 23 + 16 = 39 u; (ii) formula unit mass of Ca(NO3)2 = 40 + 14 + 48 = 102 u; (iii) molecular mass of H2O = 18 u; (iv) 'the molecular mass of NaCl is 58.5 u'. Use Na = 23 u, Ca = 40 u, N = 14 u, O = 16 u, H = 1 u. Judge each entry, correct the wrong ones with the right numbers, and state the common error in (i) and (ii).
questions.a: (i) Wrong: 2 x 23 + 16 = 62 u. (ii) Wrong: 40 + 2 x (14 + 48) = 164 u. (iii) Correct: 2 + 16 = 18 u. (iv) The number 58.5 is right, but the term is wrong; NaCl is ionic, so it is a formula unit mass. Common error in (i) and (ii): the subscript or bracket multiplier was ignored.
s: (iv) number right, term should be formula unit mass

questions.q:
A school lab in Pune has two unlabelled white solids, P and Q. P dissolves in water, not in kerosene; the bulb stays off with dry P and glows with the P solution. Q dissolves in kerosene, not in water; the bulb never glows. A label on a third bottle says 'NaCl or Na2O' and the measured formula unit mass is 58.5 u (Na = 23 u, Cl = 35.5 u, O = 16 u).
(a) Classify P and Q as ionic or covalent.
(b) Why does the P solution glow while dry P does not?
(c) Find the formula unit masses of NaCl and Na2O and the difference.
(d) Which compound is in the third bottle, and which test should the teacher record as proof?
questions.a: (a) P ionic, Q covalent. (b) In solution the ions are free to move; in the dry solid they are fixed. (c) NaCl = 58.5 u; Na2O = 62 u; difference 3.5 u. (d) NaCl, since the measured 58.5 u matches it and not 62 u; the recorded proof is the formula unit mass.
s: Part (b): ions free to move only in solution
Part (d): NaCl justified by 58.5 u match

questions.q:
A farmer in Nashik compares two nitrogen fertilisers, ammonium nitrate, NH4NO3, and potassium nitrate, KNO3. Use H = 1 u, N = 14 u, O = 16 u, K = 39 u. The farmer wants the most nitrogen for each 100 kg bought, and the two cost the same per kg.
(a) Find the formula unit mass of each.
(b) Find the mass of nitrogen per formula unit of each.
(c) Work out the percentage of nitrogen by mass in each, to one decimal place.
(d) Which should be bought, and how many kg of nitrogen does 100 kg of it carry?
questions.a: (a) NH4NO3 = 14 + 4 + 14 + 48 = 80 u; KNO3 = 39 + 14 + 48 = 101 u. (b) NH4NO3 has 28 u of nitrogen (2 atoms); KNO3 has 14 u. (c) 28/80 = 35.0 percent; 14/101 = 13.9 percent. (d) Ammonium nitrate; 100 kg carries 35 kg of nitrogen, against 13.9 kg.
s: Part (b): 28 u and 14 u of nitrogen
Part (d): ammonium nitrate, 35 kg of nitrogen
